chapters.caption: Alfred Waterhouse's terracotta palace (opened 1881) — look for the animals carved into its very walls.
chapters.directions: Enter via the Cromwell Road main entrance, which brings you directly into Hintze Hall.
chapters.text: Before you go in, stand across Cromwell Road and take in the building, because here the container is half the exhibition. The Natural History Museum opened in 1881, designed by Alfred Waterhouse, and it is quite deliberately a cathedral — a cathedral of nature. This was the vision of Richard Owen, the great anatomist who coined the word 'dinosaur': he wanted a temple to the variety of creation, grand enough to hold the natural history collections that had outgrown the British Museum. Waterhouse gave him a Romanesque palace clad in terracotta — chosen because it would survive London's sooty air — and then covered it in animals. Run your eyes along the facade: monkeys, pigeons, fish and extinct creatures are carved into the arches and columns, and there's a code to it. The west wing carries extinct species; the east wing, living ones — the building itself is an index of life and loss. Inside are some 80 million specimens, though you'll see a tiny, carefully chosen fraction; behind the scenes this is one of the world's great research institutes, with hundreds of scientists working on everything from malaria to meteorites. The galleries are colour-coded into zones — Blue for dinosaurs and mammals, Red for the Earth, Green for birds and creepy-crawlies, Orange for the Darwin Centre — and this tour threads the best of them. Come in through the main Cromwell Road entrance. You're about to meet a whale.
chapters.title: Welcome: A Cathedral of Nature

chapters.caption: Hope, the 25-metre blue whale skeleton, diving through Hintze Hall since 2017.
chapters.directions: The Dinosaurs gallery is on the ground floor to the left (west) of Hintze Hall.
chapters.text: Walk in, and look up. Suspended from the ceiling of Hintze Hall, diving toward you through the great Romanesque arches, is Hope: a 25-metre skeleton of a blue whale, the largest animal known ever to have lived on Earth. Hope's story begins in 1891, when this young female whale stranded on a sandbank at Wexford in Ireland; the museum bought her skeleton for £250, and for decades she hung in the Mammals gallery. In 2017 she was moved here, taking pride of place from a beloved predecessor — Dippy the Diplodocus, the plaster dinosaur who greeted visitors for over a century and is now out on long-term tour (a bronze Dippy, nicknamed Fern, stands in the gardens outside). The swap was a statement: out went an extinct giant, in came a living species that humans hunted to the edge of extinction and then, through conservation, pulled back — hence the name Hope. Don't rush through the hall; it's a gallery in itself. Around the bays you'll find a hand-picked cabinet of wonders: an American mastodon, an Atlantic blue marlin frozen mid-leap, one of the most complete British dinosaurs, a Mantellisaurus, and a piece of rock older than almost anything on the planet. Look up again before you leave — the ceiling carries 162 hand-painted panels of plants from around the world, and the grand staircase is watched over by a seated Charles Darwin, placed centre-stage in 2009, the bicentenary of his birth.
chapters.title: Hintze Hall: Hope the Blue Whale

chapters.caption: A Tyrannosaurus rex skull — the gallery also holds part of the first T. rex skeleton ever discovered.
chapters.directions: Return toward Hintze Hall, then cross to the Exhibition Road side for Earth Hall — or take the East Entrance route past the gift shop.
chapters.text: The Dinosaurs gallery is the museum's blockbuster, and it earns it. You walk a raised, one-way route through the age of reptiles, skeletons looming over and beside you, and the undisputed star still startles people half a century after the dinosaurs' renaissance began: the animatronic Tyrannosaurus rex, which rears up, swings its massive head and roars as you approach. It's theatre, yes, but theatre with a serious cast. Look for the genuine fossils the gallery is really about — including part of the first T. rex skeleton ever discovered, a reminder that this museum has been in the dinosaur business since the very beginning: the word 'dinosaur' itself was coined by this museum's founder, Richard Owen, in 1842. Seek out the horned skull of Triceratops, the sail-backed and the armoured giants, and the very British stories: Baryonyx, a fish-eating predator dug out of a Surrey clay pit in 1983, and the Iguanodon material that connects to Gideon Mantell, the Sussex doctor who recognised the first dinosaurs from teeth like an iguana's. The gallery does real science as it goes — how dinosaurs moved, ate, grew and raised young, and how birds are their living descendants. A practical tip: this gallery gets genuinely crowded, with a queue at peak times. If it's heaving, press on to the Earth galleries and circle back later in the afternoon, when the school groups have gone.
chapters.title: Dinosaurs: Face to Face with the T. Rex

chapters.caption: Sophie the Stegosaurus in Earth Hall — the most complete Stegosaurus skeleton ever found.
chapters.directions: Ride the escalator up through the Earth sculpture to the Volcanoes and Earthquakes gallery.
chapters.text: Now cross to the museum's east wing and change elements entirely: from life to the planet it lives on. Earth Hall announces itself with a skeleton that stops everyone for a photograph — Sophie the Stegosaurus, the most complete Stegosaurus ever found, nearly every bone real, excavated in Wyoming and unveiled here in 2014 after a mystery donor funded her purchase. Sophie stands guard over one of the great museum entrances: an escalator that carries you up through a giant metallic globe, its surface etched with the constellations, so you quite literally travel through the Earth to reach the galleries above. It's the museum's best piece of showmanship after the whale. At the top, the Red Zone tells our planet's violent story. In Volcanoes and Earthquakes you'll find the museum's most visceral exhibit: an earthquake simulator recreating the 1995 Kobe earthquake inside a shaking Japanese supermarket, tins rattling off the shelves as the floor bucks beneath you — thirty seconds that explain plate tectonics better than any textbook. Around it, the evidence accumulates: lava bombs and ash from real eruptions, seismometers tracing live tremors around the globe, and the story of how the Earth was built, layer by layer, from a molten ball to the thin green crust everything lives on. Take the escalator slowly on the way up. The view back down through the globe is a stunner.
chapters.title: Earth Hall: Through the Planet Itself

chapters.caption: The Minerals Gallery — virtually unchanged since 1881, with The Vault guarding its greatest treasures at the far end.
chapters.directions: The Human Evolution gallery is in the Green Zone, back toward the centre of the museum.
chapters.text: Tucked on the first floor of the east wing is the museum's most quietly magical room. The Minerals Gallery is the one space that survives almost exactly as Waterhouse built it in 1881: long rows of polished wooden cabinets under a barrel-vaulted ceiling painted with trees, case after case of crystals in every colour chemistry allows. Wander it slowly — amethyst geodes, pyrite suns, opals, quartz in a dozen habits — and you'll understand why generations of geologists speak of this room the way art lovers speak of the Sistine Chapel. At the far end, behind a door that looks built for a bank, is The Vault, where the museum keeps its crown jewels of geology. The treasures rotate, but the regulars are extraordinary: the Latrobe Nugget, one of the largest lumps of gold ever found, dug up in Australia in the 1850s; the Ostro Stone, the largest cut blue topaz in the world, flawless and the size of a brick; a meteorite from Mars — an actual piece of another planet you can stand a metre from — and the so-called Cursed Amethyst, a deep purple gem whose 19th-century owner wove it a legend of theft, misfortune and doom so persuasive that the museum still displays it in its little silver box, ringed with protective charms. Believe the curse or not — Edward Heron-Allen, who owned it, had it locked away and begged his daughter to throw it in the Thames. She donated it here instead. You're welcome.
chapters.title: Minerals and The Vault: Earth's Crown Jewels

chapters.caption: Gough's Cave, Cheddar Gorge — where Cheddar Man, Britain's oldest complete human skeleton, was found in 1903.
chapters.directions: Head for the Blue Zone's Mammals gallery, on the ground and first floors of the west wing.
chapters.text: The Human Evolution gallery, in the Green Zone, takes on the biggest question of all: how did we get here? It's a compact gallery, so give it your full attention — the specimens are small and the stories enormous. Start with the skull in the case that changed science before science noticed it: the Neanderthal skull from Forbes' Quarry, Gibraltar, found in 1848 — eight years before the famous Neander Valley specimen gave Neanderthals their name. Had anyone recognised what it was, we'd call them Gibraltarians. Around it, the gallery lines up our extended family: casts of Homo naledi, the small-brained, long-limbed species announced from a South African cave in 2015; Lucy-era australopithecines; the tools our ancestors knapped from flint; and the British evidence that pulls the story home. Look especially for Cheddar Man: his skeleton, found in Gough's Cave in Somerset in 1903, is the oldest complete human skeleton in Britain at around 10,000 years old — and when scientists sequenced his DNA in 2018, the results startled everyone, suggesting this Mesolithic hunter had dark skin and blue-green eyes. Beside him, the 400,000-year-old Swanscombe skull fragments show humans hunting in a warmer, elephant-roamed Kent. Interactive displays let you compare your own hand, brain and gait with a Neanderthal's. Spoiler: the family resemblance is strong, and a few per cent of most non-African genomes today are Neanderthal inheritance — you may be looking at a cousin.
chapters.title: Human Evolution: Meeting the Family

chapters.caption: The 28-metre blue whale model in the Mammals gallery — built in the 1930s and still the gallery's presiding giant.
chapters.directions: The Darwin Centre is at the museum's west end, beyond the Mammals gallery — follow signs for the Orange Zone.
chapters.text: You've met the blue whale's skeleton; now meet its body. The Mammals gallery, in the Blue Zone, is presided over by a full-size model of a blue whale, 28 metres long, built in the 1930s when no complete whale could be preserved any other way — craftsmen modelled it from photographs and measurements of real whales, and it remains one of the museum's most beloved objects. Swimming alongside it, in model and specimen form, is the rest of the mammal clan, and the gallery's pleasure is sheer variety at full scale: an African elephant at the rotunda, giraffes stooping, hippos, polar bears, and case after case of the order we belong to doing everything mammals do — flying, burrowing, swimming, hunting. This is one of the museum's older galleries, and its traditional, specimen-rich style is part of its charm; where newer galleries interpret, this one simply shows, trusting the animals to be astonishing enough. It's also a quiet history lesson in how museums used to work — many of these specimens were collected in the age of empire and expedition. Compare the two whales before you leave: the airy skeleton in Hintze Hall, all engineering and lightness, and this blue leviathan, all bulk and presence. Between them, you'll have a better sense of the largest animal that has ever lived than any film can give you.
chapters.title: Mammals: The Other Blue Whale

chapters.caption: The Cocoon, inside the Darwin Centre — eight storeys of collections and laboratories wrapped in a giant white pod.
chapters.directions: Return toward the Cromwell Road side; the Wildlife Garden is reached from the museum grounds on the west side.
chapters.text: At the museum's western end, the Victorian palace gives way to the 21st century. The Darwin Centre is the museum's working science campus, opened in two phases in 2002 and 2009, and its centrepiece is unmissable: the Cocoon, a vast eight-storey white pod, like a silkworm's casing blown up to architectural scale, floating inside a glass atrium. Inside the Cocoon are the collections you never normally see — millions of specimens, including the spirit collection of creatures preserved in jars — and the laboratories of some 200 scientists. When the visitor route through the Cocoon is open, you can wind down its ramps, peer through windows at researchers at work, and get a sense of the museum's true scale: the galleries you've walked today display perhaps one specimen in ten thousand. Even if the Cocoon route is closed on your visit, the atrium is worth the walk — the contrast between Waterhouse's terracotta and this bright white pod is the museum's whole history in one glance, and there are often scientists giving talks or showing specimens at the centre's public benches. This is also your reminder that the Natural History Museum is not really a museum with a research department attached. It's a research institute — tackling biodiversity loss, disease and planetary science — that generously lets the public wander its front rooms.
chapters.title: The Darwin Centre and the Cocoon

chapters.caption: The Wildlife Garden — an acre of British habitats in the museum's grounds, home to thousands of recorded species.
chapters.directions: Head back inside to Hintze Hall for the wrap-up — or exit from the gardens onto Queen's Gate.
chapters.text: End the tour outdoors, in the museum's most peaceful acre. The Wildlife Garden, opened in 1995 in the museum's west grounds, is a living exhibit: a carefully planted patchwork of the habitats that make up the British countryside, compressed into a city block. In a short stroll you pass through chalk downland, a reed-fringed pond busy with dragonflies and moorhens, hedgerows, meadow and a small woodland — and the astonishing statistic is that more than 3,000 species have been recorded living here, wild, in the middle of Kensington: moths, beetles, fungi, birds, bats and bees, all monitored by the museum's scientists as a baseline for urban nature. It's the museum's argument made in grass and water: you don't need a rainforest to find biodiversity; you need to look properly at what's already here. A practical note: the garden keeps seasonal hours and closes over the winter months, roughly November to March, so if the gate is locked on your visit, take that as the exhibit being honest about the British year — and peer through the fence at the pond anyway. In spring and summer, though, allow it a good twenty minutes; after the marble and terracotta, the quiet out here, with the museum's towers rising behind the trees, is one of London's loveliest surprises.
chapters.title: The Wildlife Garden: Nature, Live

chapters.caption: The grand staircase of Hintze Hall, with Darwin seated at its heart since 2009.
chapters.directions: All three exits are close: Cromwell Road for the main hall, Exhibition Road for the Science Museum next door, Queen's Gate for Gloucester Road station.
chapters.text: Let's finish back under the whale. A few parting thoughts to take with you. First, remember what this place is for: of the 80 million specimens in the building, you've seen a few thousand, and the rest are a working library of life on Earth, consulted daily by scientists from around the world — including, in recent years, researchers who identified new species from specimens collected a century ago and sitting in a drawer ever since. Second, notice how the museum's heroes have changed: Richard Owen, its founder, lost his famous argument with Darwin, yet it is Darwin who now sits on the staircase and Darwin's name on the science centre, while Owen's cathedral houses the evidence that proved evolution to the world. There's something very British, and very hopeful, about that. Third — if you have energy left, the Science Museum is two minutes east along Exhibition Road, and the V&A two minutes beyond it; South Kensington's trio of great free museums is unmatched anywhere. If the Dinosaurs gallery defeated you with its crowds earlier, now — late in the day — is your moment to go back. And if you're here on the last Friday of the month, check for the museum's Lates evenings, when the whale, the bars and the dinosaurs stay open after dark for adults only. However you end it, walk out under Hope once more. A century ago her species numbered in the hundreds; today there are thousands of blue whales again. The museum chose its symbol well.
chapters.title: Wrap-Up: Under the Whale

intro: Welcome to London's temple of the natural world. Behind this terracotta facade — part cathedral, part palace, and decorated with hundreds of carved animals — sit 80 million specimens, the most important natural history collection on the planet. You can't see it all, so this tour strings together the essentials in the order you'd naturally walk them: the great whale in Hintze Hall, the dinosaurs, a ride through the centre of the Earth, gems and cursed amethysts, our own ancestors, the second blue whale, the scientists' Cocoon, and finally the quiet of the Wildlife Garden. The museum is free and very popular; if you do the dinosaurs first or last, you'll dodge the worst of the crowds. Allow two to three hours.

location.name: Natural History Museum, Cromwell Road, South Kensington, London

mapNote: There are three entrances: Cromwell Road (into Hintze Hall, under the whale), Exhibition Road (into Earth Hall, by the Stegosaurus) and Queen's Gate (nearest the Dinosaurs). This tour starts at Cromwell Road: Hintze Hall and Dinosaurs on the ground floor, Earth Hall in the east wing, Minerals on the first floor of the east wing, Human Evolution in the Green Zone, Mammals in the west (Blue Zone), the Darwin Centre at the far west end, and the Wildlife Garden in the west grounds. Zones are colour-coded on the museum's maps.
practical: Admission is free, but book a free entry ticket online in advance to guarantee entry and skip the longest queues; members and ticket-holders have a faster line.
Open daily 10:00–17:50, last entry 17:30. The Dinosaurs gallery is the busiest room in the building — visit it first thing or in the last hour.
The Exhibition Road entrance (by the Stegosaurus) is often quieter than the Cromwell Road main entrance, and the station tunnel from South Kensington Tube leads straight to it.
The Wildlife Garden is seasonal and closes during the winter months; the Darwin Centre's Cocoon route may also vary — check the museum website on the day.
There are several cafés, a large shop, cloakrooms at the entrances, and step-free routes throughout, though the historic building has no air conditioning and gets warm on busy days.
Special exhibitions (such as Wildlife Photographer of the Year) are ticketed and sell out on weekends — book ahead if one catches your eye.
subtitle: Hope the blue whale, roaring dinosaurs, a trip through the Earth, and a cursed amethyst
title: The Natural History Museum
